profession_name: First-Line Supervisors of Construction Trades and Extraction Workers

daily_reality.summary: Construction supervisors (foremen, superintendents) directly supervise and coordinate construction or extraction crews on job sites. They manage schedules, ensure safety compliance, read blueprints, and solve field problems. Early starts (6-7 AM), outdoor work in all weather, typically 40-50+ hour weeks.
typical_tasks: Scheduling workers, assigning tasks, and coordinating crew activities
Reading and interpreting blueprints, specifications, and work orders
Ensuring OSHA safety compliance on job sites
Conducting daily toolbox talks and safety briefings
Ordering and tracking materials and equipment
Inspecting work quality and ensuring code compliance
Communicating with project managers, engineers, and inspectors
Resolving field problems and making on-site decisions
Completing daily logs, timesheets, and progress reports
key_documents: Daily field reports and progress logs
Safety inspection checklists and incident reports
Change orders and RFIs (Requests for Information)

deadlines.osha_incident_reporting: Within 8 hours for fatalities, 24 hours for hospitalizations
deadlines.osha_30_card: Required before starting supervisory work (in many jurisdictions)

daily_reality.seasonality: Construction peaks spring through fall. Winter weather slows or stops outdoor work in northern states. Year-end push to complete projects before deadlines. Extraction work may have different cycles based on commodity prices.

regulatory.summary: OSHA is the primary regulatory framework (29 CFR 1926 for construction). OSHA 30 card recommended/required for supervisors. State licensing varies. No single national certification required but many employers require specific trade certifications.

key_laws.name: OSHA Construction Standards (29 CFR 1926)
key_laws.description: Federal workplace safety standards specific to construction industry

key_laws.name: OSHA 30-Hour Construction Outreach Training
key_laws.description: Recommended/required training for construction supervisors covering safety hazards

key_laws.name: State contractor licensing laws
key_laws.description: Many states require contractor licenses for supervising construction work

key_laws.name: Local building codes and permits
key_laws.description: Municipal regulations governing construction quality and safety

key_laws.name: Davis-Bacon Act (federal projects)
key_laws.description: Requires prevailing wages on federally funded construction projects

requirements: OSHA 30-Hour Construction Safety card (strongly recommended/often required)
OSHA Competent Person designation for specific hazards (fall protection, excavation, scaffolding)

regulatory.recent_changes: OSHA increasing enforcement actions. Growing focus on heat illness prevention regulations. Silica dust exposure standards being more strictly enforced. Some states requiring Site Safety Training (SST) cards (e.g., NYC requires 62-hour SST for supervisors).

tools.summary: Mix of construction management software, field communication tools, safety equipment, and traditional construction instruments. Mobile technology increasingly replacing paper-based processes.

primary_tools.name: Blueprint and plan viewers
primary_tools.description: Digital plan viewing on tablets and phones

primary_tools.name: Scheduling and workforce management
primary_tools.description: Crew scheduling and labor tracking tools

primary_tools.name: Safety management platforms
primary_tools.description: Digital safety checklists, incident reporting, toolbox talks

primary_tools.name: Communication tools
primary_tools.description: Radios, smartphones, and messaging apps for field coordination
primary_tools.examples: Two-way radios, WhatsApp/GroupMe for crew, Procore messaging

secondary_tools: Drones for site inspection and progress monitoring
pain_points: Resistance to digital tools among experienced tradespeople
Poor cellular/internet connectivity on some job sites
High cost of technology adoption for small contractors

terminology.summary: Construction industry vocabulary combining trade-specific terms, safety language, and project management concepts.

terms.GC: General Contractor — firm responsible for overall project execution
terms.sub: Subcontractor — specialty contractor hired by GC
terms.foreman: First-line supervisor of a construction crew
terms.super: Superintendent — senior field supervisor overseeing multiple crews
terms.punch list: List of deficiencies to fix before project completion
terms.RFI: Request for Information — formal question about plans/specs
terms.CO: Change Order — modification to the original contract/scope
terms.submittals: Shop drawings, samples, or data submitted for approval
terms.rough-in: Installation of mechanical/electrical systems before walls are closed
terms.trim-out: Finishing work: fixtures, hardware, final connections
terms.toolbox talk: Brief daily safety meeting at start of shift
terms.competent person: OSHA designation: person capable of identifying hazards and authorized to correct them
terms.fall protection: Systems preventing falls from heights (harness, guardrails, nets)
terms.prevailing wage: Government-mandated minimum wage rate for public construction projects
terms.man-hours: Unit of labor measurement (one person working one hour)
terms.mobilization: Setting up equipment and personnel at a construction site

career_psychology.summary: Experience-based career with strong earning potential ($79,000-$110,000). Comes up through the trades — no degree required. High demand due to construction boom and workforce shortage (~439,000 workers needed). Physical and weather exposure are main challenges.
career_path: Apprentice or entry-level construction worker in specific trade

salary_range.union_supervisor: Often higher with benefits and overtime

fears: Worker injury or fatality on their watch
Project delays and budget overruns reflecting on performance
Difficulty finding and retaining skilled workers
Physical toll of years in construction
motivation: Outdoor work and variety every day
Pride in craftsmanship and trade skills
burnout_factors: Long hours (50-60+ hour weeks common during peak)
Stress of managing tight schedules and budgets
Dealing with labor shortages and unskilled workers

community.summary: Community organized through trade unions, contractor associations (AGC, ABC), and OSHA training networks. Strong apprenticeship tradition and mentorship culture.

associations.name: Associated General Contractors of America (AGC)
associations.type: Major trade association for construction firms and supervisors

associations.name: Building and Construction Trades Department (BCTD, AFL-CIO)
associations.type: Umbrella organization for construction trade unions

associations.name: National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER)
associations.type: Provider of construction training, assessment, and certification

online_communities.name: r/Construction
online_communities.description: Active Reddit community for construction professionals

market.summary: Strong demand. Construction industry needs ~439,000 additional workers in 2025, jumping to ~500,000 in 2026. 9% growth projected for construction managers 2024-2034. Infrastructure spending and housing demand driving opportunities.

demand_forecast.growth_rate: 9% for construction managers (2024-2034, BLS — much faster than average)

market_trends: Massive infrastructure spending (IIJA, CHIPS Act) driving demand
Severe skilled labor shortage across all trades
Technology adoption: drones, BIM, mobile project management
Growing focus on safety culture and mental health in construction
Prefabrication and modular construction changing field operations
Green building and sustainability creating new specializations
